#8919. $656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

“Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.

Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”

When I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh. Because on the one hand, when you put a bunch of personal life details online like this, being misunderstood is just part of the package. But on the other hand, if the critics could peek in and see our real lives – not just mine but those of all the Mustachians – they would have to give up their conspiracy theories and accept the fact that this stuff just works.

Because really, not much has changed when it comes to the basics. Like many MMM readers over the past twelve years, my total wealth level has increased pretty regularly.  But also like many of us, I haven’t felt the need to change very much about my spending because I was doing my best to live an enjoyable life in the first place.

How have so many people found such great success? I think we Mustachians have something that’s a bit more rare and special than standard financial advice, which is what makes it work so well:

Standard Advice: Slash your spending and make sacrifices until you reach a certain savings percentage, and beyond that it doesn’t matter, it’s all personal choice. More income? Great, that means you don’t have to sacrifice as much! FatFIRE for everyone!

Mustachianism: Cultivate a love of efficiency, creativity, self awareness, and self improvement. Use this knowledge to improve your life in all ways, including those which help you live better even as your monthly expense rate drops over time.

Well, I’ll give you some examples from my own present-day life. Things I do because I happen to enjoy them, which also happen to save a lot of money. Some of these are normal, some are silly and may end up in some future gossip magazine hit piece, but all of them happen to work for me, so the critics can be damned.

As I list each item, I’ll include an estimate of how much the activity saves me per decade, because you should always think at least in terms of decades. To make that calculation yourself, just use the “rule of 172” – take a monthly expense and multiply it by 172 to estimate how much it would compound into over ten years, if invested.

1) Fixing my own House (and everybody else’s too)

I’m a big believer in self-sufficiency, and working to build up the skills to manage the most important parts of your own life without depending on too many things (or people) that are outside of your control. In other words, one giant recipe for a happy life is simply to Become a Producer of the Things You Most Enjoy Consuming.

And in my case, I happen to love houses. I like living in beautiful, functional spaces and sharing them with friends. But most houses are ugly and poorly designed when you buy them, so I realized that I also love solving problems and redesigning old buildings to become new again. I enjoy this process so much that I spend most of my free time doing it – on both my own properties and the homes of friends.

And I love teaching other people to gain power over their own houses too. It’s amazing how great people feel as they lose their fear and dependence on outside contractors, and gain the ability to fix and maintain things with their own two hands.

Savings: An average of $20,000 per year = $287,000 per decade

You know what’s great? Having so much money that you can buy whatever you want – high quality things which get delivered to your front door the very next day.

You know what’s even better? Not buying some of those new things, and instead finding ways to share, repurpose and buy equally high quality items from other people who don’t need them any more. All while building up your own community and creating new friendships in the process.

Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and even NextDoor all have Buy Nothing groups for most areas. In the MMM-HQ community, we run a Discord server with about 200 local people, who chat around the clock on a wide range of subjects. They help each other with major projects in one channel called #diyhowto, and give away and sell things on #forsale and #buynothing.

Although our private Discord group is my favorite, I also use Craigslist regularly, and probably save (and earn) a few thousand every year thanks to the habit:

We all know that Mr. Money Mustache’s biggest contribution to personal finance is to insist that bike transportation is the best way to get around. And I still feel this way. As we learned in The True Cost of Commuting, cars cost at least 50 cents per mile to operate, while bikes are much cheaper, mainly due to reduced depreciation and maintenance costs (which are even bigger than the gas savings).

I do still use bikes (or walking) for at least 95% of my local trips these days, but because I live in the center of a small city, my life is pretty local. So this still only adds up to about 2000 miles per year, a savings of “only” $14,000 per decade.

But when you choose active transportation, there’s much more to the picture than just cutting your car expenses. You’re changing everything about your physical and mental health picture for the better, which brings us to the next point of…

Although I’m no competitive athlete, whenever I see an option to make my body work a bit harder, I usually take it. Stairs instead of elevators, running the golf course instead of using a golf cart, moving my own furniture and appliances instead of calling a mover, shoveling snow and raking leaves instead of using a machine.

When I face a decision like this, I simply ask myself the question: “Well, Mustache. Do you want MORE health and fitness, or LESS?” Putting it in that context makes the answer obvious.  Every bit helps, because when it comes to your body, the rule is pretty much use it or lose it.

But how much money does this save? There’s no real way to calculate it exactly, but I like to think of it this way: The US average health care spending is about $13,000 per person per year. My lifetime costs due to illness or medication so far have been just about zero, plus I know I’ve had more energy and greater productivity due to being healthy. Let’s just put it very conservatively and set the estimated savings and benefits at $10k per year which means

5) Saving Energy by Running my home like a Glamping Retreat

Here’s where things get a bit silly, but my level of joy is actually at its greatest.

My personality type is probably a weird combination of an engineer, a carpenter, an artsy hippie, and a mad scientist. Oh, and a devoted homebody too. Because of this, my favorite activity most days is to just run around my house taking care of things and trying new little experiments and improvements.

Sometimes I’ll cut a few big holes on on the South side of the house and install sliding doors and big windows to allow nice sunbeams and passive solar energy to get into my house and give me free heat in the winters. Other times it’s just smaller things to save energy and live more at at one with the seasons of my area:

Even taken all together, these things are pretty small – the average combined gas and electric bill for my area is about $250 per month, while my usage adds up to about $75. So while we’re only saving about $30,000 per decade for what sounds like a lot of work to most people, I consider this to be the biggest win because I enjoy living in “MMM’s Energy Efficiency Playground” so much.

“Hey, we’re having a big back yard pool party next weekend to celebrate Amy’s graduation from kindergarten, can you make it?”

“OH NOOOO!!! We will be off in at Disneyland that whole week! We planned the trip months ago, I wish we could make it!

As I type this in the height of the summer season, I really feel this effect at its fullest: almost all of my friends are off on trips, and my guest suite here at home is almost constantly full. People are traveling a lot, and many of them sound like they wish they could spend a few more of their precious summer weeks and weekends at home.

I’ll let you in on a little secret: you can! The trick is saying, “no thanks” more often to plans that involve you being away, and “yes please” to things that let you stay at home. The benefits are numerous:

Estimated Savings: Even if you replace just two weeks of travel for a family of four, with equivalent time at home you might save $5,000 per year in direct costs and a further $5,000 per year in incidental benefits like the health and local friendships. This would work out to a shocking $143,000 per decade of wealth increase!

Of course, travel is generally a good thing for broadening the life experience of you and your kids. It’s worth spending on, lavishly at times. But the key is to balance it out and be discerning, keeping the most enriching trips and pruning a few off the bottom of the list. And remembering that home time is valuable and healthy too.

And Whoa! We’ve already built up a huge list and I feel like I was just getting started.

Taken all together, we’ve already detailed things that compound to $656,000 every decade, which already more than double the median wealth that most American seniors have as they cruise nervously into their retirement years – after over 40 years of work!

And now that I’ve been writing this blog for over ten years myself, I can safely say that over $656,000 of even my most recent worth increases are directly attributable to these simple habits. The same ones many of us have been enjoying and preaching about all along, both before and after our retirement dates.

If money is in genuinely short supply, you could go a lot further than the examples in this article. And indeed, there’s a lot more laid out in this blog or the MMM Boot Camp email series.

But one of the points of Mustachianism is that you usually don’t have to try all that hard. Just tweaking your lifestyle to be slightly less ridiculous and more efficient than average is usually all it takes.

In the comments: what are your quirks and frugal indulgences? The things you do now to save money, or things you still do even after it’s no longer about the money? I often wonder how widespread this frugality-just-for-fun is. But since we Humans are a naturally curious and problem solving species in our natural state, I suspect there are many more of us out there.

I think his first point “Fixing my own House” is invaluable advice for any homeowner in HCOL areas. I live in a very HCOL city (a conscious decision that currently is worth the tradeoff for me) and bought a modest “fixer upper” for well below my neighborhoods average home price during COVID.

Boy did I quickly hit the “find out” part of that decision. I’d never touched renovations or building or fixing a home / apartment beyond mounting bike racks on my rented apartments walls. I received insane quotes for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and all the drywall repairs required for that kind of work. I did the math out for many of these projects based on the number of people and days the companies told me it would take and in many cases these companies were pulling in $300 per man-hour.

So I didn’t hire any of them. I spent an entire year learning the plumbing and electrical code for my city / state / country. I bothered the hell out of my city inspectors with questions. Made dozens of trips (sadly mostly via car) to the big box stores – eventually even started accounts with supply houses and lumber yards for better variety and deals.

In the two years I spent renovating the house, I’ve saved myself more than $300,000 (estimating the value of my time at $50/hour).

If anybody on here is considering buying a home, but isn’t willing to learn to do this stuff themselves, I think renting might be the more Mustachian decision if the alternative is paying for somebody else to do this work. I also don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.

(1) My grad school room mate and I loved new clothes but really couldn’t afford them. That $50/month difference meant we were stoked by our new sweater and usually pocketed the savings the other months.

(2) Buy wool clothing. It’s more durable, needs to be washed less, and you can have a smaller wardrobe (which takes up less space, saving you money in storage/heating costs). Even better buy used wool clothing.

(3) Books. I love reading and go through upwards of 50+ books a year. Buying those new at a bookstore would be $30-$50 a month! Instead, I use Libby through my library and constantly have a multitude of books on hold. So yes, I need to wait, but honestly, it’s not that bad if you just had a great book come up that you’ve been waiting for. Slow gratification :)

I have finally settled on washing hair 2-3x a week, using tiny amounts of shampoo and conditioner only when necessary means I can save 5 bottles of each a year.

#8917. Science Finds that Dairy May Not Lead to Excess Fat as First Thought

For a long time, the public were cautioned against regular dairy food consumption, but a recent study from the University of Toronto, published by the Journal of Nutrition, appears to show that frequently delving into eggs, milk, and cheeses, could actually benefit your health and won’t make you fat. Here’s why.

In the ‘70s, a war on saturated fat consumption encouraged us to avoid products like whole milk, butter, and cheese because of the high levels that they contain. Then wellness culture in the new millennium further derailed the case for diary, citing inflammation, acne, and disrupted hormones on this food stuff. Of course, some people are lactose intolerant, and have problems processing dairy food, but the Toronto study has challenged the campaign against dairy, with some surprisingly edible results.

74 overweight adults undertook a 12-week study and were randomly assigned to one of three groups:

All the groups were counseled on healthy eating, so that they could manage their food intake. At the completion of the trial, the team took measurements including body weight, composition, cholesterol, blood markers, and metabolic health.

In both of the regular high fat dairy eating groups, the participants experienced improvements in their blood pressure while consuming a greater amount of protein, calcium, and vitamin D than the first group. Importantly, neither their waistlines nor BMI suffered. “Those that had three servings of dairy didn’t have adverse levels of blood cholesterol or lipids or evidence of insulin resistance,” explained Gerald Harvey Anderson, who was the lead author and works in the Faculty of Medicine at the University of Toronto.”

With full-fat dairy containing more saturated fat than reduced fat products, how could this be? The experts believe that dairy’s combination of fats and protein is what makes it a positive food. “With dairy products, it’s got two proteins, casein and whey, that are bound together with fat and with nutrients mixed in,” said Anderson. The “Dairy Matrix Hypothesis” suggests that the physical structure of dairy determines how the body processes its nutrient profile.

Of course, ice cream, milkshakes, and other treats that contain a ton saturated fat as well as massive amounts of sugar is a different story, but the Toronto study said its results with natural dairy products showed that  “Neither treatment nor time affected waist circumference, fat and fat-free mass, resting metabolic rate, fasting blood cholesterol, and urine creatinine.” The team concluded that “Frequent and daily consumption of full-fat dairy as part of a healthy diet is consistent with CFG (Canada’s Food Guide).”

This news also adds to another promising benefit of dairy, that was reported earlier this year. The American Academy of Neurology showed that those who regularly ate high fat cheese presented a 13% lower risk of dementia overall, and a 29% risk of vascular dementia. Cream was also associated with a 16% lower risk of all-type dementias.

The Toronto study found dairy to be a significant source of magnesium and potassium to boot. “The results align with the conclusion of an expert group that there is no evidence to support the avoidance of high-fat dairy in diets,” it said.

#8915. How to Correctly Add Forward and Reverse Lunges into Your Legday Workouts

When it comes to strengthening your legs, building muscles in your lower body, and improving all-round balance, lunges are a great move to lean into, but what is the difference between the forward and backward lunge? In a recent Instagram post, IFBB Pro, endurance athlete, and transformation coach Petar Klancir demonstrated the details.

Take a step in the right direction with these unique lunges.

“What is the difference?” asked The Croatian Colossus, who has built an Instagram base of more than one million followers thanks to his informative training videos. In essence, both of these variations are compound movements, so they tax multiple muscle groups at the same time. Whether you lunge forward or backward, you’ll be working the quads, hamstrings, calves and core. You will also flex the hips either way. But what does change is the emphasis placed on each muscle, and how they build your legs in different ways, as Klancir showed.

“Front step lunges target the quads more, due to the mechanics of the exercise,” explained Klancir. “The emphasis is on stepping forward, which requires the quads to control the impact of the foot’s landing. And there is a high degree of flexion.”

The quads take the majority of the load with forward lunges, because the mechanics that Klancir mentioned, require the quads to negotiate the lowering, and then lift your center of mass and return you to the starting position.

Tip: To avoid knee stress, be sure not to step out too far forward on the lunge. At the bottom of the lunge, your knee should only just be ahead of your chin.

“Back step lunges target the glutes and hamstrings,” said Klancir. “Due to emphasized hip-hinge movement.”

Reverse lunges are often considered easier to execute, because the front foot remains flat on the floor, providing a greater foundation and less requirement for core balance. They are also less stressful on the knee, because the load is shifted by the hamstrings and glutes to a greater extent than the quads.

Tip: Keep the front foot stable by keeping knee over ankle at all times.

For a complete leg blaster, your can try both movements by focusing on form. Then, once you are comfortable with your foot placings, you can build in some additional hypertrophy by adding a pair of dumbbells to the overall load.

#8912. How Rucking Helped ‘Outlander’ Star Sam Retford Become Battle Ready

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Sam Retford, who is known to millions of Outlander: Blood of my Blood fans as Dougal MacKenzie, looks very comfortable on a show that requires him to navigate the unpredictable Scottish terrain, and there’s a good reason why. Not only does Retford love the great outdoors, but he’s also vastly experienced in a variety of skills. From riding a horse to cave diving, or rucking to offroad bike racing, this actor is as able as they come. So, staying still for just a second, Retford tells M&F why Outlander is such a personal and professional high, and how his favorite pastimes informed the role and his physique.

Now living in Glasgow, Retford’s love of adventure was passed down through blood. “My mum was a proper ranch cowgirl,” says Retford, who was born in Australia. “She has ridden horses all around the world, so she taught me to ride.” The star says that he loves nothing more than to get a bunch of pals together and go exploring, and has recently biked in The Himalayas, crossed the rivers of Amazonia, and cave dived around the United Kingdom. When the news came down that Retford would take up the role of Dougal MacKenzie and battle it out in 18th century Scotland, he was understandably all-in.

While most actors stay within the confines of a gym to ready for their roles, Retford added to his indoor workouts by acclimatizing to his new filming environment. As War Chieftain Dougal MacKenzie, Retford wanted to get a feel for the rugged highland landscape. “I wanted this guy to be physically capable,” he tells M&F, noting that he practiced rucking up and down the hills with a weighted backpack. “Even going and sleeping in the heather. I really wanted to build a physique capable of doing these long winter treks, but remain flexible enough to be agile in battle, to be strong enough to carry heavy loads—so everything had to be functional.”

The type of physique required to hunt and survive in the wilds of Scotland would not require a six-pack or be akin to an underwear model, so Retford wanted to build his character with authenticity. “I wanted him to have a big strong back and strong legs,” says the actor. “Okay, he can, lift but can he swing a sword around as well?”

Sam Retford earned a second-degree black belt in Taekwondo in his youth and understands the importance of exercise for agility and injury prevention. He also likes to swing the Indian Mace Bells for balance. But in the gym, his workouts include plyometric moves that require explosive power, such as box jumps. When lifting weights, the star focuses on time under tension and replicating proper form while squatting or making an overhead press.

The star also introduced instability into his lifting elements, for example with elevated platforms or unilateral movements in order to prepare him for the uneven ground outside. Still, the actor says that ultimately, the best way to prepare for his sprinting and fighting scenes was to run in the woods and climb trees. “Just moving about on set and staying warm,” he recalls.

Fans of Outlander: Blood of My Blood will have noticed that the physicality has leveled up in Season 2. For example, Dougal MacKenzie becomes embroiled in a serious battle in Episode 5 and must be rescued from being trapped underwater in Episode 6. Fortunately, the enthusiastic adventurer is more than comfortable with holding his breath. In Episode 2, Dougal also found himself in a fistfight with Brian Fraser (played by Jamie Roy).

Retford wants people to know, however, that progress is individual, takes time, and is not as easy as some social media accounts would like you to believe. He is also keen to point out that it takes a team of stunt coordinators, special effects wizards, lighting, and audio technicians to make any actor appear at their best. “You’ll notice I do quite a lot of shield work and headbutting, as opposed to sword fighting,” he explains. “That’s because I’m a lefty, and my right-handed combat is not very good. So, I have to keep the sword well and truly sheathed for a lot of it, to not cut anyone’s fingers off!”

Blood of My Blood no doubt the dream job for this thrill seeker. “Just to be out there in the cold, in the thick of it, running around, swinging swords. I mean, it’s a beautiful type of physicality, and it’s an amazing thing to call your job. So, I try never to complain. I’m always grateful.”

With Retford more than open to battling through a third season of Outlander: Blood of My Blood, the talented performer is also producing an upcoming documentary in Uganda and also has an eye on traveling to Mexico. “The key is to just say yes to crazy things,” he beams.

Season 2 of Outlander: Blood of My Blood premieres can be streamed via Starz.

When an American joins any branch of the United States military, they repeat an Oath of Enlistment to make the commitment official.

I do solemnly swear that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same; and that I will obey the orders of the President of the United States and the orders of the officers appointed over me, according to regulations and the Uniform Code of Military Justice. So help me God.

On November 12, 2026, 64 men and women ventured to the Rayburn Office Building of the U.S. Capitol to take that oath and enter the Air Force and Space Force Delayed Entry Program. This swearing-in was the climactic moment of the second annual National Signing Day, an event hosted by the Air Force’s 317th Recruiting Squadron.

The concept of this event came from retired Air Force Master Sergeant and M&F Senior Military Editor Rob Wilkins, who said the idea was inspired by watching his son’s announcement for where he was going to play college football.

Wilkins explained, “I was watching this take place and thought to myself, ‘We should be doing something like this for the military.’”

Wilkins’ idea became a reality thanks to several people he worked with, including Congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska, Air Force Senior Master Sergeant Matt London, and others within the 317th. It made what was already a significant moment in the lives of these future service members even more memorable for them and their families who accompanied them.

Staff Sergeant Maddalyn Secrist was one of the recruiters on-hand for the event and was very involved with making the 2026 event a success. Secrist shared that having this on Capitol Hill took something local to the DMV area and gave it a sense of national awareness.

“It gives it more of a public view and gives these Airmen and Guardians the recognition that they need.”

Prior to their swearing-in, each person’s name was announced as they went to the table to sign on the dotted line and have their photo taken, reminiscent of the high school athletes who announce where they will play in college. Each new recruit was cheered by family, friends, and fellow American citizens as well as members of the Trump Administration like Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Military Community and Family Policy Stephen B. Simmons and recently appointed Executive Director of the President’s Council on Sports, Fitness, and Nutrition, Jacob Phillips.

Among those new recruits was Kevin McAllister, who was one of the older members of the group. At 35 years old and with a family tradition of service, McAllister knew that being physically prepared was a must, which is why he committed to longer runs and more intense training in preparation for the day. He also had to mentally dedicate himself to the process and suggests others who may be considering service do the same.

“I had to find the right mindset. There was a lot of running and calisthenics, but it taught me how to use different muscles,” he said. Even though he was fully prepared to take the oath, being in the Capitol definitely added a level of gravitas to the day.

“We are surrounded by the place where laws are made. The history of the United States is here. Just getting to add this to my family legacy makes me look at the flag differently.”

Bacon addressed the group and offered words of gratitude and encouragement that could be traced back to his own 30-year military career before entering the House of Representatives. He also shared wisdom that could be beneficial to people from all walks of life, whether they are in the military or not.

“Be the best at the job you’re going to get,” Bacon advised. “Learn that job inside and out so your boss can go, ‘I can trust that person.’”

There is no official word on future Signing Day events, but Secrist hopes that recruiters can use highlights or social media posts from this day to inspire their own applicants and create a similar experience to showcase why being a part of the Joint Force is so special.

Secrist said, “We think other recruiters can see this event and get inspired to do something like this in their own squadrons.”

To learn more about the Air Force or Space Force, go to airforce.com or spaceforce.mil.

#8904. JJ Spaun Got His Swing Back After a Misdiagnosis Nearly Wrecked His PGA Career

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

PGA star John Michael “JJ” Spaun has been at home with the golf clubs since he was gifted that first plastic toy set at age 3. But while the young protégé followed in his mother’s golf-playing footsteps, and furthered them by making progress in the PGA, a mysterious health issue would begin to derail his game.

Spaun sat down with M&F to discuss his initial Type 2 diabetes diagnosis, and how finally being discovered as Type 1 brought him back to greener pastures.

“I would say, in the majority, golf was a pretty easy sport for me to pick up,” says Spaun. “But I think I battled with what time and effort I wanted to put into it as a kid. Growing up in Southern California, other sports were pulling me in. Skateboarding was a huge presence at the time. I wanted to do what the other kids were doing culturally, which was skateboarding and extreme sports.”

In his youth, Spaun played a variety of sports aside from golf, including skateboarding, bicycling, baseball, basketball, and hockey. But while he did eventually fully embrace golf, his other experiences began to pay off. “I think those sports all played a role in my development, in my mechanics,” says Spaun. “Like hand-eye coordination, footwork. My swing coach, who I have been with for around six years, is a firm believer that skateboarding really developed my footwork for my golf swing even as a child. He considers my feet to be my superpower.”

JJ Spaun has just completed his 10th season with the PGA. He turned professional in 2012 and earned his first PGA Tour Card in 2016, but the players’ game began to take a downturn in 2018. He struggled with consistency and even lost his tour card during the 2020-21 season, where he placed 174th in the FedEx Cup rankings. Since the summer of 2018, Spaun found himself almost unable to complete a round of golf.

“I was 28 at the time,” he recalls. “I remember putting on my belt and running out of holes to put the notch in, so my belt was now too big for me. I suffered with severe thirst at night, and then frequently urinating, like, three or four times every night. I started losing weight very rapidly.”

Initially chalking all this up to a demanding golf season, Spaun decided to see a doctor after weighing himself and realizing that he’d inexplicably lost another 20 pounds in just a couple of months. The athlete was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes and hoped that the treatment would help him return to his prior form on the golf course. But that wasn’t to be.

“After three years, losing 50 pounds, going down to 155 pounds, I hadn’t weighed that since high school, so I finally got advice from an endocrinologist,” shares Spaun, who was then diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes, rather than Type 2.

Sadly, with 90% of diabetes sufferers having Type 2, medical advances for detecting Type 1 have been slower to emerge. Type 2 is often triggered by obesity, whereas Type 1 is thought to be more of a genetic issue causing the immune system to attack insulin producing cells in the pancreas. “They felt sorry for me, telling me that I was Type 1, but I said this is great, because I’ve been living miserably,” says Spaun. “My energy was at an all-time low. My golf was going down the drain. And now I had a real solution.”

Finally gaining the correct diagnosis in 2021, Spaun started insulin therapy. “In a matter of weeks, I could feel the strength coming back,” says the top golfer. “I was able to eat things without restricting my glucose range, as you do with Type 2. I started to feel better and things started coming together.”

Losing so much weight took time to overcome, however. “Your mechanics and your movements are off,” explains Spaun. “I’m glad to be handling things well. It’s definitely a challenge, but I’ve got all the support in the world to really make it as easy for me as possible.”

Incredibly, with the weight coming back and his treatment working well, Spaun had his breakthrough season in 2025, including a major victory at the 125th US Open. Spaun tells M&F that he uses a Dexcom G7 continuous glucose monitor to keep his levels in check and has recently switched from insulin injections to a pump system known as the Omnipod 5. “It’s been a game changer for me,” he shares.

In September 2026, Spaun was also able combine his love of traveling to England with his passion for golf, winning the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth, and even donating a portion of his winnings to the Addington Fund, a British Charity that supports farming families. The golfer tells M&F that he discovered the financial hardships that many UK farms face during his holidays in the Cotswolds, where discovered the popular Prime series, Clarkson’s Farm.

“I’m the type of guy that likes to put in the work, because I’m a strong believer that you get out of this game what you put in,” says Spaun. But with the official season now over, the able athlete can look ahead to more family time, and another trip back to England.

No doubt, JJ Spaun is a highly decorated athlete with an even promising future, but living with diabetes has taught him that being present in the moment is more important than any trophy, so we conclude our interview and Spaun heads out on the school run.

#8902. How Reverse-Grip Lat Pulldowns Helped Jay Cutler Build an Even Wider Back

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

Mass monster Jay Cutler, who claimed the title of Mr. Olympia on four occasions between 2006 and 2010, was never afraid to step away from the barbell if there was an efficient way to sculpt his back. Recently, the bodybuilder revealed that he liked to begin each back session with cable reverse-grip pulldowns. Here’s why.

“This was always the first exercise I started my back routine with,” confirmed Cutler in a recent video for his 5.7 million IG followers.

Techniques used by Jay Cutler to string together 25 consecutive top 2 finishes.

Utilizing a supinated (underhand) grip, you’ll primarily tax the lats while also recruiting the biceps and mid back. For many, the supinated grip is more comfortable on the shoulders than the pronated (overhand) grip. So, seated at the cable station, you’ll replicate a similar movement with the upper body to a chin up as you lower the bar. This grip also allows for heavier loads, making it perfect for adding upper body mass.

Tip: Keep your torso still and pull with the elbows until the bar is lowered just under your chin. Don’t pull any further down, or the load will shift to your forearms and shoulders.

“When you do something, reverse grip, it’s going to give you more flexion in those lats. It’s going to allow you to pull a little deeper and engage certain fibers,” explained Cutler who, as a competitive bodybuilder, was all about lifting heavy weights to create a winning physique.

In his video, Cutler kept the distance between his hands a little over shoulder width. “Pull down, focus on 12 repetitions,” he added. The Olympia icon also explained that the reverse grip lat pulldown was essential to building the winged appearance of his lats. “So, when I was doing that front double bicep (pose), it really yanked those lats out,” shared the legend. “And created that great V-taper.”

For Jay Cutler, the reverse grip lat pulldown was key to building muscle thickness. To try it for yourself, avoid using momentum and concentrate on the muscle contraction instead, as you lower the bar. Then slowly allow the bar to return skywards for additional time under tension.

Nick Walker is expected to hit the Arnold Classic stage in March, and if this heavy upper-body workout is anything to go by, “The Mutant” could be unstoppable in Columbus, OH, next year.

With the Arnold Classic now on his mind, the 2026 Mr. Olympia winner is hoping to top last year’s second place and rule this stage like he did last September at the Olympia. And, to get there, it appears that The Mutant is willing to push past his own superhuman limits. This was evidenced by a recent Instagram reel, in which Walker recorded a brutal but brilliant upper body session for his 2-million-plus followers.

With Olympia runner-up Samson Dauda speculated to enter, and Andrew Jacked confirming that he will try to defend his 2026 Arnold Classic trophy, Walker understands that each and every rep counts.

The 2026 Mr. Olympia found the ultimate success this time around with his outer sweep.

Walker’s video shows some seriously heavy sets, with the aim of reaching failure, so you should conduct some feeler sets to find the correct weight for you. For added safety, The Mutant is also spotted by IFBB Pro, Andy Paredes. “I’m not big on partners, but homie trains hard,” quipped Mr. Olympia in his IG caption.

The session started with the seated incline dumbbell press, a move that builds the shoulders, upper chest, and triceps. “Best chest on stage,” encouraged Paredes as Walker got ready to leave it all on the gym floor. “No weaknesses this year.”

Next up was the seated chest press machine, hitting the entire chest, shoulders, and triceps. Using the machine means that Walker can target these muscle groups effectively, while a traditional bench press requires the recruitment of the core for stabilization.

For his third exercise, The Mutant upped the anti with his chest dips, adding a plate suspended from his waist by a chain. And, if you are wondering what separates a chest dip from a triceps dip, it’s all about the positioning. Notice that Walker’s head and chest are forward, whereas triceps dips are characterized by a straighter torso. This way, the big man is activating the chest and anterior deltoids at the front of his shoulders

Moving on to the standing lateral raise machine, The Mutant turns his attention to the lateral (side) and rear deltoids, providing his upper body with a broader topline. Notice how he raises and then lowers the handles in a slow and controlled motion for added time under tension.

For his final exercise, Walker continues to build winning arms with standing barbell bicep curls, blasting those biceps and engaging the core to remain stable. Despite the heavy load, the 2026 Mr. Olympia once again concentrates on quality muscle contractions and time under tension.

To replicate these reps for yourself, aim for 3 sets of 8 to 12 reps on each exercise. The added weight on the chest dips is optional, but be sure to go heavy, taking in at least one feeler set to avoid injury. This may be a brutal workout, but the muscle building benefits could be brilliant.

#8896. Air France-KLM Flying Blue → Tahiti Business Class

The only points path to nonstop business class service to French Polynesia

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Champagne in hand, watching the sun melt into the ocean from 35,000 feet. In eight hours, you'll land in Papeete — French Polynesia's gateway to overwater bungalows, turquoise lagoons, and the kind of trip people save their whole lives for. And you got here on points. This is the Air France business class seat to Tahiti, and it represents one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. Not just because of where you're going — though Tahiti is bucket-list by definition — but because of the staggering gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you'll pay in miles. **The math will genuinely stop you in your tracks.** A business class ticket from Los Angeles (LAX) to Papeete (PPT) on Air France regularly retails between **$5,000 and $12,000 per person**. That's the cash reality. But with Flying Blue miles — Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program — you can book the same seat for as few as **88,000 miles**. At the high end of retail pricing, that's a value of **13.6 cents per point (CPP)**. Even at the low end, you're extracting **5.7 CPP** from miles that most programs value at 1–2 cents. In the ChooseFI community, we talk constantly about optimizing every dollar toward financial independence — and a redemption that turns 88,000 transferable points into a $5,000–$12,000 experience is about as powerful as it gets. Here's what makes this feel different from your average business class booking: Air France operates a **Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner** on this route, featuring a modern, premium business class cabin with direct aisle access for every seat, noise-reducing windows, better humidity levels, and that unmistakably French touch in service and catering. You're not just flying in a recliner — you're flying in a genuine lie-flat pod on one of aviation's most celebrated aircraft. And this is the only nonstop option. Air France is the **sole carrier operating nonstop LAX–PPT** service. That's not a coincidence — it's a pricing inefficiency baked into the route's geography, and it's exactly the kind of structural advantage the ChooseFI community knows how to exploit.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program is the only way to book the only nonstop flight between Los Angeles and Tahiti using points — and that program happens to offer some of the most generous award pricing in the world.

Flying Blue uses a dynamic award pricing model, meaning costs fluctuate based on demand and availability. That sounds like a disadvantage — and sometimes it is. But here's the inefficiency: Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards every single month. These are fixed-price award seats on select routes, discounted 25–50% off standard award pricing. When Tahiti appears as a Promo Reward destination (which it does periodically), the pricing drops dramatically — and crucially, Promo Reward tickets eliminate carrier-imposed fuel surcharges entirely.

Fuel surcharges on Air France-operated flights are normally moderate, but they're real — they can add $200–$500 to an award ticket. Promo Rewards wipe those out. This is the pricing inefficiency: Flying Blue is essentially subsidizing this cabin to drive demand, and you can capture the subsidy.

Here's the beautiful part for ChooseFI members: virtually every major transferable points currency sends to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. That means:

The Chase, Amex, and Citi transfers are instant, which matters enormously when you're racing to lock down a business class award seat before someone else grabs it. You find the seat, you confirm it's available, then you transfer — because once points leave your bank, they don't come back.

This is the single most important rule in booking award travel, and it's especially critical here. Flying Blue's award availability on the LAX–PPT route is genuinely limited — this is a popular route to a popular destination on a single aircraft. You do not transfer points speculatively. You find confirmed availability on flyingblue.com, verify the seat count and pricing, then immediately transfer from your Chase, Amex, or Citi account (all instant) and book.

Flying Blue allows open-jaw routing, meaning you could potentially fly into Papeete and out of another South Pacific destination if Air France serves it — giving sophisticated travelers a way to build a multi-destination itinerary without paying for a separate return trip to your origin city. It's a small but meaningful piece of flexibility in a program that doesn't always offer it.

This is a moderate-difficulty booking. The steps themselves aren't complicated — but the sequencing matters enormously. Follow this in order.

Go to flyingblue.com and use the award search tool. You do NOT need a Flying Blue account to search — but you will need one to book, so create a free account if you haven't already. Search LAX → PPT in business class. Flying Blue's calendar view lets you scan across multiple departure dates, which is essential for spotting availability on a route with limited award seats.

Tip: Flying Blue's booking window opens 359 days in advance. For a route this popular and this capacity-constrained, searching at the 11-month mark is strongly advised. Set a calendar reminder for exactly 359 days before your target travel dates.

On the first of each month, Flying Blue releases its new Promo Rewards. These are fixed-price, reduced-cost awards with no fuel surcharges. Bookmark flyingblue.com/en/earn-spend/flying-blue-promo-rewards and check it monthly. If Tahiti appears, act immediately — Promo Reward availability disappears fast.

Once you find available dates and seats, note the exact miles price shown at checkout. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing means the cost you see on Monday might differ from Thursday. Screenshot the search result with the price clearly visible. This is your confirmation that the award is priceable before you transfer points.

Now — and only now — transfer your points:

Transfer the exact amount you need — no more, no less.

Return to flyingblue.com, complete the search again with your now-funded account, and book. Have your passport and traveler details ready. Pay any taxes/fees (usually $50–$150 on non-Promo awards; near-zero on Promo Rewards) with a travel rewards credit card to earn additional points.

Award availability on this route moves quickly. If your target dates are sold out:

Flying Blue uses dynamic award pricing, which usually makes award charts unpredictable. But the monthly Promo Rewards program creates a fixed-price overlay that dramatically undercuts the dynamic rates. When Tahiti appears on the Promo Rewards list, business class pricing drops 25 to 50 percent below standard and fuel surcharges are eliminated entirely. Air France is the sole operator of the LAX to PPT nonstop — no other airline flies it — which means Flying Blue is the only loyalty program with direct booking access to this route. This combination of route exclusivity and periodic promotional pricing is what makes this a genuine sweet spot rather than just a good redemption.

Card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's make this concrete. Imagine a couple planning their 10th anniversary trip to Bora Bora in the spring of 2026. They want to start the trip right — meaning lie-flat seats over the Pacific, not a middle seat in economy for a nine-hour flight.

The cash price: Air France business class from LAX to PPT in spring typically runs $6,500–$9,000 per person round-trip. For two people, you're looking at $13,000–$18,000. That's a car payment for most families. Even if it's in the travel budget, it's a brutal number to justify when you're pursuing financial independence.

The points price: 88,000 Flying Blue miles per person, round-trip in business class. For two passengers: 176,000 Flying Blue miles total, plus approximately $200–$300 in taxes and carrier fees (less if you catch a Promo Rewards release, where surcharges are waived entirely).

The CPP math: At $8,000 in cash value against 88,000 miles, you're extracting 9.1 cents per point — nearly 5–9x the baseline value of transferable points currencies. That's the ChooseFI lens: every point you've earned on everyday spending just multiplied in purchasing power.

What you'll actually experience: You check in at LAX and are directed to the business class line — a detail that still feels quietly luxurious no matter how many times you've done it. Once onboard the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner, your seat converts to a fully flat bed of approximately 6 feet in length. The cabin's reduced cabin pressure and higher humidity mean you arrive in Papeete meaningfully less fatigued than you would in economy — important when you have a connecting boat ride to Bora Bora ahead of you.

Air France's catering reflects its French heritage: expect a proper multi-course meal service, a curated wine selection, and warm bread — not a foil-wrapped tray. The flight is roughly 8–9 hours nonstop, so there's time to genuinely sleep, watch a film, and arrive rested.

For a couple using points they accumulated from normal household spending over 12–18 months, the $16,000 in combined cash value they didn't spend is the real number — and the one that matters most on the path to FI.

Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards on the first of every month. Set a phone reminder. These promotions offer 25–50% off standard award pricing AND eliminate fuel surcharges. On a Promo Rewards release, an 88,000-mile business class award could drop to as low as 44,000–66,000 miles with no surcharges. That's the difference between good and extraordinary. Don't miss a cycle.

Flying Blue's booking window opens 359 days in advance. The LAX–PPT route operates a single daily nonstop on a single aircraft — meaning business class inventory is finite and competitive. If you're targeting holidays, school break windows, or peak Tahiti season (July–August), mark your calendar to search at the 11-month mark.

Flying Blue permits open-jaw routing, meaning you could potentially fly into PPT and return from a different city — or fly from a different origin. This flexibility can reduce deadhead positioning flights and help families traveling from cities other than Los Angeles build more logical itineraries.

This is the cardinal sin of award booking. Transferred points cannot be reversed. Never move miles to Flying Blue until you have confirmed award availability on your exact dates with a price you've screenshotted. Chase, Amex, and Citi all transfer instantly — use that speed advantage after you've confirmed the seat exists.

Flying Blue's dynamic pricing means the same route can cost meaningfully different amounts day-to-day and even hour-to-hour. Don't assume the price from your earlier search is locked in. Always verify at checkout before transferring.

Because Flying Blue accepts transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, and Bilt at 1:1, your earning strategy is flexible. Focus on a single flexible currency — the Chase Sapphire Preferred or Reserve for Ultimate Rewards, or the Amex Gold/Platinum for Membership Rewards — and let everyday spending build toward the 88,000-mile target over 12–18 months.

Marriott transfers to Flying Blue at 3:1 — meaning 264,000 Marriott points become 88,000 Flying Blue miles. Unless you have a massive Marriott balance you can't use elsewhere, this is an inefficient path. Stick to the 1:1 partners.

This redemption is purpose-built for couples and families planning a landmark trip to French Polynesia — an anniversary, a honeymoon, a milestone birthday, or simply the trip you've been telling yourself you'd take "someday." If Tahiti or Bora Bora is on the life list, this is the redemption that makes it financially defensible from a FI perspective.

Minimum requirements: 88,000 Flying Blue miles per person for round-trip business class, plus approximately $100–$300 in taxes (less on Promo Rewards). For a couple, plan for 176,000 transferable points minimum.

For the ChooseFI community, this redemption represents the travel rewards philosophy at its best: redirecting the value of everyday spending into genuinely transformative experiences, without derailing the path to financial independence.

Register for free at flyingblue.com. Enable email notifications for Promo Rewards announcements. Set a calendar reminder for the 1st of each month to check the new promo routes the moment they are released.

Use the Flying Blue award search calendar view to scan business class availability on the LAX to PPT route across multiple dates. Check both standard pricing and Promo Rewards pricing. Do not transfer any points until you confirm available seats.

Once you confirm award space, transfer the required miles from Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant), Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant), Capital One (1-2 days), or Bilt (1-2 days). Only transfer after confirming availability.

Complete the booking on flyingblue.com as soon as your miles arrive. Select your preferred lie-flat seat through the seat map. For couples, choose adjacent seats in the business cabin. Promo Rewards availability is limited and can disappear within hours.

Standard dynamic pricing typically runs around 88,000 miles one-way in business class from LAX to Papeete. When Tahiti appears on the monthly Promo Rewards list, that price can drop to 44,000 to 66,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges — a savings of 25 to 50 percent.

Tahiti is not guaranteed every month. Flying Blue rotates destinations across its network. You may see Tahiti appear several times per year, especially during shoulder season. The key is having your points ready and checking on the 1st of every month so you can act immediately when it appears.

The nonstop Air France flight to Tahiti only departs from LAX. However, you can book a connecting itinerary through flyingblue.com that includes a domestic connection to LAX on the same award ticket. Alternatively, book a separate positioning flight to LAX using a different program.

No. One of the defining benefits of Promo Rewards is that fuel surcharges are eliminated entirely. You pay only the mile cost plus minimal taxes and airport fees, typically $60 to $100 per direction. This is a significant advantage over standard Flying Blue pricing, which can include carrier-imposed surcharges.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Flying Blue to Tahiti in business class is a genuinely unique sweet spot because no other loyalty program can book this route. The only nonstop from the US to French Polynesia operates exclusively on Air France out of LAX, and Flying Blue is the only way to book it with miles. At Promo Rewards pricing of 44,000 to 66,000 miles one-way, you are getting a $6,500 or more experience for transferable points that most ChooseFI members already hold. Set your monthly reminder, keep 80,000 to 100,000 points in reserve, and book the moment Tahiti appears on the promo list. #8894. Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.

As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs. Trump should not be consuming much of our time.  Sure, we do our research and cast our votes but after that we move right on to focus on other things within our own circle of control.

But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money. Your money, the economy in general, and the overall wealth of the nation.

Politicians are already not known for being the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to technical stuff like science, technology, or economics. But this year the discourse has become particularly dumb, as our candidates try to manipulate undecided voters in swing states with ideas that are based on irrational emotions rather than sound economic sense.

For one particularly funny example, you may have noticed that the competing party (Trump in this case) is attacking the incumbents (Biden/Harris) over the “bad economy.” When in fact the US economy is stronger than it has ever been, with the lowest unemployment we’ve ever seen as well.

It’s hard to imagine a better situation than we have right now, and in fact the recent bout of higher inflation is a sign that things have been going too well, and we needed to step on the brakes with the help of higher interest rates.

But somehow the people still seem to believe that we have a “bad” economy. Take a look at this Gallup poll showing that while most people (85%) are doing really well right now, they assume that it’s just their own good fortune – only 17% believe the economy is doing well.

This is mathematically impossible, because if most people are doing well, that’s the definition of a good economy! And suspiciously enough, this widespread wrongness correlates quite nicely with the rise of social media misinformation.

So the politicians and the news have been doing the opposite of what they should be doing in an ideal situation (sharing accurate information). And sure, we can always just ignore their speeches and go on with our lives. But when it comes to economics, knowledge is power (and money). The more accurately we understand how things really work, the wealthier we will all become.

So with all that in mind, I hereby present you with my list of the…

Top Dumb Things Politicians Want You To Believe About The Economy

If there’s a recession, the opposition party likes to blame it on the current president. If the economy is booming, the current president likes to give himself (or possibly soon herself) credit for all of that success. But really, the US economy is way too big – and thankfully way too free – for the president to control or really even influence all that strongly.

In reality, our economy is a gigantic machine which converts labor and materials into things like iPhones, hospitals and pumpkin pies. And although we’re the biggest economy at 26% of the planet, we are still heavily influenced by that much bigger 74% of economic activity that the other 7.6 billion people on Earth are busy producing everywhere else.

When we have our inevitable little boom and bust cycles, they are mostly caused by the normal cycle of irrational exuberance (and greed) like the 2007 housing boom, followed by brief periods of extreme fear and pessimism like the 2008-2012 financial and housing crash.

The government does play a role too, by setting tax rates and other rules. But the effects of these policies are usually so delayed and unpredictable, that you can’t draw a straight line between today’s president and today’s economy. In other words, the government does its best to adjust the rudder on our giant ship, but in the short term our economy lurches around on the waves and storms of the ocean.

This one is especially funny to me, as our candidates feign sympathy for the hard life of middle class Americans, who now face higher borrowing costs on their credit cards and car loans and mortgages. They claim they will fight to bring the interest rates down. Trump even goes as far as bullying our Federal Reserve board members (who can only do their jobs if we allow them to function as independent experts) and suggesting that he would take over the whole department, if elected.

The real story is that while monetary policy would be a terrible tool to leave in the hands of a sitting president (see Argentina), it does function as an excellent set of gas and brake pedals for the economy if used properly. When things slow down and unemployment gets too high, a cut to the interest rates will produce a boost in everything from new jobs to stock prices. But if things get too hot, you get rapid inflation which can mess up the system.

3: Inflation has Made Life Harder for Americans (and the President Can Magically Reverse it)

This line of reasoning is even dumber than the last one. For a couple of years after the Covid era, we had rapid inflation. It was caused by a rare combination of a goods shortage caused by things like factory closures and remote work, plentiful demand from government stimulus spending and low interest rates. These factors have since ironed themselves out, and inflation is back down to an ultra-low 2.4%.

But most significantly, wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%. So even after all that inflation, we are still doing just fine. But the candidates are still bickering over inflation as if it’s an actual problem, and even worse promising to “bring prices back down”. And they’ve managed to convince the electorate that “higher wages and prices” is the same thing as “a bad economy”. Which is just plain wrong.

Bonus dumbness: politicians also occasionally blame “greedy corporations” for increasing prices to hoard profits. While price increases are totally acceptable in a market system (as a business owner you are free to set prices wherever you like), in reality it doesn’t usually happen because our markets are too competitive. For example, a recent deep analysis from NPR showed that no, grocery stores haven’t made any windfall profit at all off of this recent bout of Covid-fueled inflation.

One important thing that has changed over the past ten years is that US house prices and rents have both risen much faster than general inflation and even wages. On the positive side, interest rates have also risen which tends to make houses feel more expensive and is supposed to help bring house prices down. But it hasn’t happened yet which means we have the double whammy of higher prices and higher interest costs for mortgage borrowers.

The dumb part is that our candidates are proposing things that would make the problem even worse, like subsidies for first-time homebuyers or schemes to reduce the interest rates. When really the solution is to increase the supply of housing, which I personally think will happen if we stop putting up roadblocks for homebuilders (myself included) to build housing.

Things like faster and cheaper permits, less onerous and expensive building codes, eliminating suburban-style zoning and setback and car parking rules, and changing laws so that NIMBYs no longer get any say over what other people do with their own land could all help reduce the cost of building a house by about 50%, quickly and permanently.

5: The President Controls Gas Prices, and They Are Currently “High” and We Want Them Lower

Ahh, gasoline! The most ridiculous of things to worry about and the fuel for many of MMM’s rants since 2011.

First of all, on an inflation-adjusted basis, gasoline is still about the same price as it was in 1950: in the $3-4 range per gallon, in today’s dollars.

Secondly, it is so cheap that even with our huge inefficient American vehicles, the average household is still only spending 2.5% of their disposable income on the stuff! (The funny part is that they spend many times more on the rest of the car ownership experience while thinking gas is the part that is expensive)

Third, gasoline has been obsolete for almost a decade now. You can get a used electric car for less than the price of a comparable used gas car, or if you’re a fancypants money waster like me, new EVs are also cheaper than their gas counterparts. You get a faster, nicer car that almost never needs maintenance OR gasoline, and save money.

So why are we even still talking about this antique fuel of a previous era? Why aren’t the candidates also arguing over the price of Kodak film or typewriters or fax machines?

6: The Economy is Something We Should Even Worry About

The funniest part about all this economic talk is that we’re focusing on the wrong thing. While hard work and business and advancing the frontiers of human knowledge are all fun things, the reality is that we passed the point of having “Enough” decades ago. When the American middle class complains about how hard we have it these days, it’s like a bunch of overfed people at a buffet wishing they could just have one more flavor of donuts stacked onto the table.

Yes, we have income and wealth inequality so that the rich tend to get richer more quickly. And yes, we should keep that in check with a somewhat progressive tax system because a more equal society tends to be a more peaceful and happy one.

But have you noticed that as the rich people get richer, they don’t get any happier? It’s because after you pass the point of “Enough”, adding more money doesn’t really help much.

And “Enough” is much more defined by your mindset (and your collection of life skills) than your paycheck. So if the politicians really cared about improving our happiness and wellbeing, they’d be preaching the Principles of Mustachianism rather than pandering to the specific requests of coal miners or billionaires.

But alas, winning an election is a very different thing than proposing stuff that is actually best for the country. And for that reason, we cast our votes for the best party and then tune back out until the next election.

Agreed! I think this is the biggest economic myth that needs to be addressed. Autarky is the end goal of all these tariffs, and it has negative economic consequences that seem to be missing from what the politicans say. Without the ability to trade, countries lose the benefits of specialization and comparative advantage. This leads to higher prices for in country consumers and a lack of diversity in available goods. Autarky stifles innovation and technological progress by isolating a country from global competition and advancements. An autarkic system is also more vulnerable to domestic economic shocks, such as natural disasters or supply disruptions, because it cannot rely on imports to balance shortfalls. Autarky reduces a country’s economic growth potential by cutting off access to international markets, foreign investment, and trade-driven employment opportunities. Finally, it risks diplomatic isolation, as trade restrictions often result in retaliatory measures from other nations, further limiting a country’s global economic and political influence. While autarky may appeal in terms of self-reliance, the downsides—higher costs, reduced growth, and vulnerability—make it unsustainable in the modern country.

1. “Government deficits don’t necessarily cause inflation. They are funded by the sale of T-bills and bonds.”

Yes, but if demand for those bonds is weak, the central bank steps in as the lender of last resort, printing money to purchase them, which can lead to inflation.

2. “Even an expanding money supply does not dictate the inflation rate. As we saw last year, we can have inflation even when the money supply shrinks, and this year we have much lower inflation even with a growing money supply.”

Yes, but inflation often lags behind changes in the money supply—it can take time for new money to fully circulate and impact prices.

3. “Moderate inflation is NOT bad and does not destroy purchasing power (unless you keep your wealth all in cash).”

Inflation does destroy purchasing power. Investing in assets that grow faster than inflation, like stocks or real estate, can keep you ahead of it. They don’t avoid inflation, they just try to beat it.

I think hybrids were great as a transition technology, because they helped our gas cars become more efficient back when batteries were too expensive to make an affordable all-electric car.

For example, in 2013, electric car battery packs cost about $780 per kWh to build, meaning my Tesla Model Y’s 80 kWh pack alone would have cost $62,000!

Today (2024 as I write this) that battery pack number is about $100, so my battery is only $8k of the car’s price. And since an electric car no longer needs an engine, transmission, exhaust system or all the other junk that comes with combustion, we now see electric cars have become LESS expensive than gas cars of equivalent quality/performance (the model Y is in the low $40s brand new, and under $30k used)

With the combination of easy+cheap home charging plus a bunch of nationwide fast charging networks (Tesla’s is still the best by far), there is no reason to have to settle for a hybrid – unless you’re shopping in the cheaper end of the used market. An under $10k used Prius with low miles is still a great frugal car if you can find one!

Avoid Nissan Leafs since their charging standard is no longer used and their batteries are air cooled, leading to far more degradation than other EVs that have active cooling. If you’re looking at Chevy Bolt’s make sure the battery modules were repaired per the recall. One of the best things about them is that your house is your “fuel” station. If you don’t have at home charging available it can be more of a challenge (unless your work has chargers).

Our 2014 Leaf that we bought used for a song in 2019 is still doing exactly what we need it to do – around town car, usually under 10 miles per day (eBike would be even more economical, but I kinda like my climate control here in the very hot, very humid southeast). If you’re needing to do a lot of long-distance driving, then yeah – Leaf’s, particularly older ones aren’t a great choice.

Agreed on at-home charging still the best way – public charging is expanding, but paid public charging is often as expensive as gasoline.

7) The President does not control the stock market

The effect of a Trump or Harris win on the stock market will be pretty much neutral, just as it was in 2016 when Trump won or 2020 when Biden did. Lots of short term noise, but no real effect over the years. The stock market will continue going UP as long as our economy continues to grow.

Of course, a bad enough president/government CAN steer our giant ship into an iceberg if they push through enough dumb policies. Tariffs and trade wars (currently promised by both sides) are one such dumb idea. Another one is behaving erratically so that companies have less trust in our economic and legal systems – stable institutions and predictable policies matter if you want big companies to continue investing and hiring people in your country.

But in general, our big corporations have such a big say in US politics that both parties need to be pretty business-friendly in order to get anything passed.

And although some corporations do plenty of bad things at the margins, I’m still in favor of a business friendly country that is not overly regulated. It’s why I moved here in the first place!

I would add to this, that the only thing that would have a major (potentially permanent effect) on the stock market is if our form of government changes. That is, if we tragically go from a democracy to authoritarianism. This has been shown to torpedo the stock market in other countries it has happened to, both very acutely in the short term as well as in the long term.

If that doesn’t happen, the stock market could have a major correction that has nothing to do with who is in office, and mostly just from the fact that valuations are extraordinarily high.

Fed Chair appointees, 3-letter-agency party switches, congressional changes (see: presidential coat tails), tax cuts versus tax increases, and on and on… all affect the stock market tremendously.

Here are some Mustachian principles I think apply to farms, ranches, and people who live in rural areas.

Trade the pickup truck for a smaller, less expensive, and preferably used vehicle that does the job better and drive it as little as possible. For everything else, buy a bike or small (used) sedan. There are shades of rural, but a lot of transportation needs can still be met by bike or electric bike. I rode my ebike about 40 miles yesterday to run errands in the city. I grew up in the sticks, and I’d have had a lot more freedom if I’d had an ebike. An electric cargo bike may able to be substituted for a four-wheeler or pickup truck for a lot of on farm transportation. The bike I have can basically carry the weight of two people. If you’re moving a dozen 40lb bags of feed around, that’s a max of four trips by electric cargo bike. Bikes are low, so loading one is faster and easier than throwing bags up into a pickup truck bed.

#8891. 5 Pain-Free Arm-Building Alternatives to Barbell Curls

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The barbell biceps curl is arguably a cornerstone of arm day as well as a favorite among gymgoers.

But even with its popularity in the weightroom, there are subtle issues that could come from barbell curl, the main one being a straight bar could be uncomfortable for your wrists.

Unlike dumbbells, which offer more freedom of movement, the barbell doesn’t. That fixed grip might not vibe with your wrists and forearms as the weight gets heavier. With form issues like wrist hyperextension, questionable grip width, and a little too much body English, your wrists may rebel.

This doesn’t mean you should ditch it at the first sign of wrist discomfort. Sometimes, adjusting your grip, cleaning up your form, or checking your ego at the gym door is all that’s needed to start curling without wrist pain.

But sometimes, the barbell and your wrists will not get along.

Next, I’ll break down four common reasons barbell curls strain your wrists and what you can do about it. Then I’ll cover five biceps-building alternatives that let you pump up without the pain.

Here are four common reasons barbell curls bother your wrists and how to fix them.

Unlike dumbbells, a barbell locks both hands in a fixed position. Depending on your forearm anatomy, mobility, and grip width, this position may cause wrist discomfort. A barbell leaves little wiggle room, and your wrists may tell you all about it.

Quick Fix: Adjust your grip width for more comfort, or switch to a reverse grip.

As the load gets heavier or you become more fatigued, wrist hyperextension may happen. Instead of maintaining a wrist and forearm alignment, the bar pulls the hands backward. That adds extra demands on a body part that’s already working hard.

Quick Fix: Think knuckles in line with your forearms, and do a partial wrist curl to get your hands in that position.

There’s a time and place for body English, but if it causes unnecessary discomfort by pulling your wrist out of neutral during the curl, reconsider your strategy.

Quick Fix: Lighten the load, cut the set short when excessive momentum takes over, or use a three-second eccentric to slow things down.

Your forearms stabilize your wrists, and if you’ve already done a lot of grip work, your wrists may be tired before you begin. When your forearms and wrists fatigue, your grip may weaken, your wrist position may change, and your biceps will be left unsatisfied.

Quick Fix: If your grip gives out, do direct biceps work earlier in your workout with lighter loads, different grip positions, or the alternative exercises below.

If the form fixes didn’t work, it’s time for the alternative. A good alternative trains the biceps hard while addressing what made barbell curls uncomfortable in the first place.

Angled grips, neutral grips, and even overhand grips may feel better depending on your wrist and forearm anatomy. For example, an EZ bar reduces the amount of supination required, while hammer curls keep your palms facing each other.

Dumbbells, ropes, and resistance bands give your hands and wrists more freedom of movement than a barbell.

Look for exercises that keep your wrists neutral, let you control the lifting and lowering phases, and maintain biceps tension. Dumbbells, cables, and bands each feel different but may let you control the weight better without sacrificing gains.

The bottom line: A good barbell curl alternative should solve your wrist problem without creating a new one.

With that covered, here are five exercises that let you keep building bigger biceps without being married to the barbell.

Each exercise addresses one or more of the problems we discussed earlier, so choose wisely. Also, keep a mirror handy.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from the barbell’s fixed position.

The EZ-bar curl is the closest alternative to the barbell curl without locking the wrist in place. Its angled handles allow your forearms to sit in a slightly more neutral position, which many lifters find more comfortable than the barbell.

Form Tip: Choose a hand position that feels comfortable, and keep your wrists neutral.

Solves: Discomfort from the palms-up grip.

If you’ve been hammering the palms-up position, it’s time to switch. Using a palms-down grip shifts the exercise’s emphasis, placing greater demand on the brachioradialis and brachialis while the biceps still get the attention they deserve. The reverse curl provides a different stimulus and gives you another grip option if wrist pain is an issue.

Form Tip: Keep your elbows close to your sides, curl without body English, and lower with control.

Solves: The difficulty of keeping your wrists aligned during barbell curls.

The rope-cable hammer curl combines the wrist-friendly benefits of the dumbbell hammer curl with a touch of cable magic. This variation gives your wrists and hands more wiggle room, letting you adjust your hand spacing throughout the curl. The cable also provides constant resistance throughout the range of motion, enhancing biceps development.

Form Tip: Attach a rope to a low cable pulley and stand tall with your palms facing each other. Curl the rope toward your shoulders, then let your hands separate at lockout.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from a barbell’s fixed grip.

If barbell curls hurt your wrists, the answer may be to lighten the load and switch resistance types. That’s where the looped resistance band curl earns its place. Unlike a barbell, which provides the same external weight throughout the rep, a resistance band’s resistance increases as it stretches.

And don’t mistake bands for beginner-only equipment. Take a challenging set to near muscular failure with good form, and your biceps will thank you.

Form Tip: Grip the sides with your preferred grip, keep your wrists aligned, and curl toward your shoulders. Lower slowly without letting the band snap your hands back.

Solves: Wrist discomfort from limited freedom of movement.

Unlike a barbell, dumbbells let you rotate your forearms as you curl, moving from a neutral grip at the bottom to a palms-up position near lockout. This rotation is more joint-friendly while still engaging the biceps’ two primary functions: elbow flexion and forearm supination.

Form Tip: Start with dumbbells at your sides, palms facing inward. As you curl one dumbbell toward your shoulder, rotate your palm up. Squeeze your biceps at the top, lower under control, and repeat with the opposite arm.

Sets & Reps: 2–4 sets of 12-15 reps per side

Your biceps cannot tell the difference between a barbell, dumbbell, resistance band, or cable machine. They only care about tension. If that tension comes from a barbell and your wrists are annoyed, why keep hammering it when you have options?

If the form fixes above didn’t work, these five alternatives will help you train for gains without the pain.
